141021.title: Add CompositePodGroup garbage collection finalizer protection and int…
141021.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature
/wg workload-aware-scheduling
/sig scheduling

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Implements garbage collection finalizer protection for `CompositePodGroup` objects to enforce hierarchical, bottom-up cleanup:

- **Admission**: Extends the `PodGroupProtection` admission plugin (`plugin/pkg/admission/scheduling/podgroupprotection`) to mark newly created `CompositePodGroup` objects with the `scheduling.k8s.io/compositepodgroup-protection` finalizer.
- **Controller**: Extends `PodGroupProtectionController` (`pkg/controller/scheduling/podgroupprotection`) to index `PodGroup` and `CompositePodGroup` objects by `spec.parentCompositePodGroupName`.
- **Lifecycle Invariants**: When a `CompositePodGroup` is marked for deletion, the controller retains its finalizer while any child `PodGroup` or `CompositePodGroup` still references it as a parent. The finalizer is dropped only after all child groups have been removed, ensuring deletion proceeds leaf-to-root (`Pod` -> `PodGroup` -> child `CompositePodGroup` -> root `CompositePodGroup`).
- **Testing**: Adds full integration test coverage in `test/integration/podgroupprotection` verifying multi-level hierarchical deletion and finalizer protection.

This PR is stacked on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142387!

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-scheduling/6012-composite-podgroup-api/README.md

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Stacked PR on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142387!

- Extends the existing `PodGroupProtection` infrastructure without altering standard `PodGroup` protection semantics.
- Uses `spec.parentCompositePodGroupName` indexers in the shared informer cache to evaluate parent-child references without API server queries.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Add garbage collection finalizer protection (`scheduling.k8s.io/compositepodgroup-protection`) for CompositePodGroup objects to ensure hierarchical bottom-up cleanup of pod groups.
```

142202.title: DRA consumable capacity + CEL: fix name comparisons and lookup
142202.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When the ResourceClaim requested "driver.example.com/bandwidth" and that DRA driver published the capacity as "bandwidth", the request failed. Same for the inverse case.

A less likely problem existed when a DRA driver flipped between publishing with and without its own driver name as prefix: the allocation result stored literally what came from the driver at the time of allocation, which then wouldn't be considered after flipping to the other format.

Nothing prevents DRA drivers and users from publishing resp. requesting the same capacity with and without driver name prefix. Validation could prevent this for ResourceSlices (driver name is known) but doesn't. It's probably also not worth doing because DRA drivers are trusted and  can trivially avoid this; validation would just add overhead. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142218 makes sure that DRA driver behave well.

Lookup for constraints resolves this conflict via "fully-qualified wins". Consumable capacity and CEL resolution was random (last one in map iteration wins), now also prefers fully-qualified.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140650

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The fix is to normalize names (drop redundant prefix) before comparing. To support downgrades, the allocation result is written with the simpler name without the driver name as prefix because that is what was written in practice before.

I have included making the consumable capacities and CEL capacities/attributes lookup deterministic in this PR. The one about CEL could also be a separate PR, but it seems related enough to not add that review overhead.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
DRA consumable capacity: requesting capacity had to be done with the capacity name exactly as published by drivers, i.e. typically without the driver name prefix. When requesting with a fully-qualified name, the request failed. Now both unqualified and fully-qualified names work. A related, less likely problem existed when a DRA driver changed how it published capacity and some capacity was allocated already.
```

#### AI usage disclosure:

YES: test cases were written manually, then AI was used to fix the code based on a description what the solution should look like.

140880.title: [KUBELET]: Filter scoped link-local DNS servers
140880.body:
## What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig node
/area kubelet

## What this PR does / why we need it

Fixes an issue where kubelet propagates unusable scoped IPv6 link-local nameservers into pods using `dnsPolicy: Default`.

Today, when kubelet reads the node's resolver configuration, nameserver entries are copied into the pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` verbatim. If the node contains a scoped IPv6 link-local nameserver such as:

```text
nameserver fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0%3
```

that exact value is written into every `dnsPolicy: Default` pod.

The scope (`%3` in this example) refers to an interface index that only exists in the node's network namespace. Regular pods run in their own network namespace, so the scoped address cannot be used from inside the pod, resulting in DNS failures such as:

- `network unreachable`
- `invalid argument`

This also affects workloads (such as CoreDNS when configured with `dnsPolicy: Default`) that inherit the node resolver configuration and forward DNS queries using `/etc/resolv.conf`.

### This change

This PR filters inherited scoped IPv6 link-local nameservers **only** for pods that satisfy:

- `dnsPolicy: Default`
- `hostNetwork: false`

The filtering removes nameservers that:

- are IPv6
- are link-local unicast (`fe80::/10`)
- contain a scope zone (for example `%3` or `%eth0`)

Examples:

| Nameserver | Result |
|------------|--------|
| `1.1.1.1` | ✅ preserved |
| `2001:4860:4860::8888` | ✅ preserved |
| `fe80::1` | ✅ preserved |
| `fe80::1%3` | ❌ removed |
| `fe80::1%eth0` | ❌ removed |

Host-network pods are **not** modified because they share the node network namespace and can legitimately use scoped link-local addresses.

The filtering is performed in the kubelet pod DNS generation flow rather than in `parseResolvConf()`, keeping the resolver parser responsible only for parsing while making the filtering decision where pod networking context is available.

## Which issue(s) this PR fixes

Fixes #140844

## Special notes for your reviewer

### Unit tests

Added unit tests covering:

- IPv4 nameservers are preserved.
- Global IPv6 nameservers are preserved.
- Scoped IPv6 link-local nameservers with numeric zones are removed.
- Scoped IPv6 link-local nameservers with interface-name zones are removed.
- Unscoped IPv6 link-local nameservers are preserved.
- Mixed nameserver lists only remove the scoped link-local entries.
- Malformed nameserver values remain unchanged.
- `dnsPolicy: Default` with `hostNetwork: false` filters inherited scoped IPv6 link-local nameservers.
- `dnsPolicy: Default` with `hostNetwork: true` preserves them.
- Other DNS policies retain their existing behaviour.

### Manual validation

Built kubelet from this branch and configured it to use a resolver file containing:

```text
nameserver 1.1.1.1
nameserver fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0%3
nameserver 2001:4860:4860::8888
options timeout:1 attempts:1
```

#### Scenario 1

Pod configuration:

```yaml
dnsPolicy: Default
hostNetwork: false
```

Result:

```text
nameserver 1.1.1.1
nameserver 2001:4860:4860::8888
options attempts:1 timeout:1
```

The scoped IPv6 link-local nameserver was correctly removed.

#### Scenario 2

Pod configuration:

```yaml
dnsPolicy: Default
hostNetwork: true
```

Result:

```text
nameserver 1.1.1.1
nameserver fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0%3
nameserver 2001:4860:4860::8888
options timeout:1 attempts:1
```

The scoped IPv6 link-local nameserver was correctly preserved because the pod shares the host network namespace.

These tests verify that:

- only normal `dnsPolicy: Default` pods are filtered,
- host-network pods retain the existing behaviour,
- IPv4 and global IPv6 nameservers remain unchanged.

## Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed kubelet so that pods using `dnsPolicy: Default` no longer inherit scoped IPv6 link-local nameservers (for example `fe80::1%3`) from the node resolver configuration unless the pod uses the host network namespace.
```

141108.title: DRA: avoid deadlocks in ResourceSlice controller Update and kubelet plugin shutdown
141108.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

With `ReconcilePoolWithName` set, `Controller.Update` rejects resources that contain other pools. It reports this through `ErrorHandler` while it holds `c.mutex`. The `ErrorHandler` docs mention replacing the slices as one option, but a handler that does this by calling `Update` blocks on the same mutex. If the previous resources had pools, the worker blocks too, so publishing stops and `Stop` never returns.

A kubelet plugin hits the same deadlock one level up. `Helper.PublishResources` holds the helper's mutex while it calls `Update` or starts the controller, so a `HandleError` that calls `PublishResources` waits for that mutex forever.

The first commit moves the check from `Update` into `syncPool`, as suggested in review. `Update` stores the resources and no longer calls `ErrorHandler`. The worker reports each other pool with the controller's context, without holding a lock, and without retrying.

Other pools are neither published nor validated, and the `ReconcilePoolWithName` pool is synced as usual. Because `Update` always stores the resources now, initial resources with other pools no longer leave the desired state nil, which could make `syncPool` panic.

The second commit fixes a related deadlock during shutdown. On master, the helper's shutdown holds its mutex while `Controller.Stop` waits for the worker. A `HandleError` that calls `PublishResources` at that moment waits for the same mutex. This can happen on master for any error that the worker reports, and the first commit adds the pool error to them. The shutdown now releases the mutex before it stops the controller.

The docs of `ErrorHandler`, `HandleError`, and both `ReconcilePoolWithName` options describe the new behavior.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

N/A

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- The review also suggested validating only the synced pool. This PR does that only with `ReconcilePoolWithName`, where other pools are never published. Without it, an invalid pool still blocks all pools. Otherwise a device that moves out of a pool whose new content is invalid would stay in the old slices and also show up in the new pool, so it could be allocated twice. The `invalid-other-pool-blocks-create-slice` case checks that an invalid pool still blocks the others.
- Behavior change with `ReconcilePoolWithName`: resources with other pools replace the desired state instead of being dropped. The `ReconcilePoolWithName` pool follows them, so its slices are deleted when it is missing. Each other pool gets its own error. The old message said "expected exactly one pool", which was wrong because an empty pool set is allowed.
- A handler that calls `Stop` blocks, because it runs on the worker that `Stop` waits for. That was already the case for other errors from the worker, and the docs now say so.
- `resourceslice` tests: `TestControllerSyncPool` gets cases for other pools, a missing or invalid `ReconcilePoolWithName` pool, no pools, and the default-mode case above. `TestControllerUpdateReconcilePoolWithNameValidation` is removed because `Update` no longer validates. `TestControllerUpdateErrorHandlerCanReplaceResources` replaces the resources from the handler. It fails, instead of hanging, if the handler runs synchronously or under `c.mutex`.
- `kubeletplugin` test: `TestStopWhileHandleErrorPublishes` runs in a `synctest` bubble and fails right away against the old shutdown code.
- Each commit passes `go test -race` for `resourceslice` and `kubeletplugin`, and `hack/verify-golangci-lint.sh` is clean. The DRA integration tests pass too, although they do not set `ReconcilePoolWithName`.
- The bug comes from #137365, which added `ReconcilePoolWithName` in v1.36. release-1.36 and release-1.37 have the same code.
- Found by reading the code and reproduced in unit tests, not seen in a real deployment.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
DRA: fixed a deadlock when an `ErrorHandler` calls `Update`, or a kubelet plugin's `HandleError` calls `PublishResources`, in response to pools that do not match `ReconcilePoolWithName`. Such resources now replace the desired state instead of being rejected; the other pools are reported to the error handler and are not published. Initial resources with other pools no longer cause a panic. Also fixed a deadlock when a kubelet plugin's `HandleError` calls `PublishResources` while the plugin stops.
```

YES. This PR was written in part with the assistance of generative AI. Claude Code helped with the locking analysis, the code and tests, and this description.

141213.title: DRA ResourceSlice: reject multi-term per-device nodeSelector
141213.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Both `ResourceSliceSpec.NodeSelector` and `Device.NodeSelector` are documented with "Must use exactly one term", but validation only enforces that for the slice-level field. For a device, `validateDeviceNodeSelection` calls `ValidateNodeSelector`, which requires at least one term and has no upper limit, so a device selector with two or more terms is accepted.

The allocator cannot merge such a selector. When `createNodeSelector` reaches one, it returns an error:

```go
default:
    // This shouldn't occur, validation must prevent creation of such slices.
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unsupported ResourceSlice.NodeSelector with %d terms", len(nodeSelector.NodeSelectorTerms))
```

The error is not wrapped with `ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`, so the DynamicResources Filter returns it as an error instead of rejecting that one node. The scheduler then stops checking the remaining nodes and fails the scheduling attempt, and retries can hit the same error for as long as the device keeps the selector.

This PR adds the missing term count check to `validateDeviceNodeSelection`, with the same error as the slice-level check.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #141212

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Compatibility comes from the atomic `spec.devices` ratchet in #141644. Tightening the device-list validation is safe on a downgrade, since older releases still accept the list, and on an upgrade, since an unchanged `spec.devices` stays valid. An update that leaves the list alone, such as a pool generation bump, keeps a stored multi-term selector. Any change to an entry revalidates the list, so an invalid selector has to be corrected. An earlier version of this PR had its own per-device ratchet, which #141644 replaced.

Allocator-side handling of already-stored malformed selectors was considered in #141214 and is not being pursued. This PR is limited to API validation and does not change allocator behavior.

Tests:
- `TestValidateResourceSlice`: a device selector with two terms is rejected, one with no terms gets the same two errors as the slice-level `bad-empty-node-selector`, and one with a single term is accepted.
- `TestValidateResourceSliceUpdate`: a stored two-term selector survives a pool generation bump, is reported when an attribute is added to its device or another device is added to the list, and is accepted once fixed down to one term.

The four rejection cases fail without the fix. The generation, added-device and fix cases fail, in that order, if node selection is checked on every update, only for the devices that changed, or against the old devices instead of the new ones.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed ResourceSlice validation to reject a per-device `nodeSelector` with more than one node selector term, as it already does for the slice-level `nodeSelector`. Allocating a device with such a selector could make pod scheduling fail with an error. A ResourceSlice that already stores such a selector can still be updated as long as `spec.devices` is unchanged.
```

141644.title: DRA ResourceSlice + ResourceClaim[Template]: reject qualified names with more than one slash
141644.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`validateQualifiedName` (handwritten) and `resourcesQualifiedName` (declarative)
both split a `resource.k8s.io` qualified name on `/` and switch on the number of
parts, handling only 1 and 2. A value with two or more slashes matches neither
case and is returned with an empty error list, so it bypasses every check the
two-part case performs -- not only the slash count, but the empty-prefix and
empty-name checks as well.

Both validators currently accept all of these:

| input | errors before | errors after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a/b/c` | 0 | 1 |
| `a/b/c/d` | 0 | 1 |
| `/a/b` | 0 | 1 |
| `a//b` | 0 | 1 |

The two validators do not cover the same fields on `resource.k8s.io/v1`.

Handwritten `validateQualifiedName` is called on the `Device.Attributes` and
`Device.Capacity` map keys only. Through `validateFullyQualifiedName` it also
reaches `matchAttribute`, `distinctAttribute` and `partitionTypeAttribute`.
`capacityKey`, `requests` and `consumedCapacity` are typed `QualifiedName` but
nothing called the function on them and they carry no format marker either.
`capacityKey` is now checked in `validateNodeAllocatableMapping`, so a malformed
key reports the format error rather than `NotFound`. `requests` and
`consumedCapacity` are left alone, they are covered by #140563.

Declarative `resourcesQualifiedName` is unexported and is only called from
`ResourceFullyQualifiedName`, so it reaches just the three fields tagged
`+k8s:format=k8s-resource-fully-qualified-name`: `matchAttribute`,
`distinctAttribute`, and `partitionTypeAttribute` (that one behind
`DRAPartitionableDevicesType`). `type QualifiedName` carries no format marker, so
the map keys and `capacityKey` have no declarative counterpart at all.

`DeclarativeValidationBeta` has defaulted on since 1.36, so where the two do
overlap both are active and neither backstops the other.

It is not only cosmetic. `parseQualifiedName` in
`staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/cel/compile.go` splits on the
first slash only, so a stored `a/b/c` attribute key is exposed to CEL as domain
`a` and identifier `b/c` -- an identifier that still contains a slash, which a
device selector cannot address.

Both functions get the missing `default` case, emitting the same message, so the
two stay equivalent and the declarative/handwritten mismatch metric stays at 0.

On ratcheting: the declarative path already skips unchanged values, since the
generated validators short-circuit on `oldValueCorrelated && op.Type == Update`.
That covers `matchAttribute`, `distinctAttribute` and `partitionTypeAttribute`.

On the handwritten side the ratchet sits on `spec.devices`. That list is
`+listType=atomic`, so the generated validation compares the whole list and
revalidates every device once anything in it changes; the handwritten validation
now does the same, and the two agree on what an update grandfathers. A
ResourceSlice that already stores a non-compliant key stays updatable while its
device list is untouched, for example when only the pool generation changes.
Adding or changing any device reports the stored key. The per-device comparisons
of `attributes`, `capacity` and `taints` are subsumed by the list comparison and
are gone.

The per-device node selection check also reads `spec.perDeviceNodeSelection`,
so it moves out of `validateDevice` into `validateDeviceNodeSelection` and runs
when either the device list or that field changes. Flipping
`perDeviceNodeSelection` on an unchanged list therefore checks only the node
selection fields, and does not revalidate what the generated code covers.

The other two handwritten call sites need nothing. `validateDeviceConstraint`
runs on create only, because `validateDeviceClaim` is reached from
`ValidateResourceClaim` and `ValidateResourceClaimTemplate` and both update
validators treat the spec as immutable. In `validatePartitionTypeAttribute` the
`validateFullyQualifiedName` call is a guard rather than a check: it returns
early and appends nothing, so a stored malformed name produces no error. All
three cases have update tests.

The two TODOs describing this gap, added in #134602, are removed.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

No issue filed; the gap was documented in-tree by the TODOs this PR removes.

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Beyond the tightening itself, the only behavior change is where the update
ratchet sits: `capacity` and `taints` were compared per device, and are now
covered by the one comparison of `spec.devices`.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Creating or updating a resource.k8s.io object with a qualified name that contains more than one slash, such as a device attribute key `a/b/c`, is now rejected. Objects that already store such a name remain updatable as long as the field holding it is left unchanged; for a ResourceSlice, as long as `spec.devices` is unchanged, since any change to that atomic list revalidates every device in it.
```

/wg device-management
/area api-validation

141742.title: tainteviction: observe pod deletion latency in seconds
141742.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig scheduling

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`deletePodHandler` records the pod deletion latency with:

```go
metrics.PodDeletionsLatency.Observe(float64(time.Since(fireAt) * time.Second))
```

`time.Since` already returns a `time.Duration` in nanoseconds, so multiplying by `time.Second` scales it by a further 1e9 instead of converting to seconds.

`taint_eviction_controller_pod_deletion_duration_seconds` is documented as "Latency, in seconds, ..." and uses buckets from 0.005 to 240. With the current code the observed values are:

| actual latency | observed             | expected |
| :------------- | :------------------- | :------- |
| 5ms            | 5000000000000000     | 0.005    |
| 1s             | 1000000000000000000  | 1        |
| 9s             | 9000000000000000000  | 9        |
| 10s            | -8446744073709551616 | 10       |
| 20s            | 1553255926290448384  | 20       |
| 30s            | -6893488147419103232 | 30       |

Below roughly 9.2s every observation lands in the `+Inf` bucket. Above that the multiplication overflows int64 and wraps around, so the recorded value is arbitrary. Negative values count in the lowest bucket, so a slow eviction can look faster than 5ms. `_sum` is meaningless in all cases.

`DeviceTaintEvictionController` already does this correctly in `pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction.go`:

```go
tc.metrics.PodDeletionsLatency.Observe(float64(podDeletionLatency.Seconds()))
```

This PR makes `TaintEvictionController` do the same and adds the regression test the package was missing, which is why this went unnoticed since the controller was split out in KEP-3902.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142617

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The test calls `deletePodHandler` with `fireAt` 10s in the past and checks that exactly one sample of about 10 seconds was recorded. 10s is above the ~9.2s overflow point. With the change in `taint_eviction.go` reverted, it fails with:

```
--- FAIL: TestPodDeletionsLatencyObservedInSeconds (0.01s)
    taint_eviction_test.go:1049: observed latency = -8.441319545709552e+18 seconds, want between 10 and 11
```

Verified on linux/arm64 with golang:1.26: `go test -race ./pkg/controller/tainteviction/ -count=1` passes, and `go vet` and `gofmt` are clean.

#141311, opened earlier, makes the same one-line change, and #141568 includes it as part of the retry-queue work.

The metric is ALPHA, so the corrected values are not a compatibility concern, but anyone graphing or alerting on it will see the series change from `+Inf`-only or arbitrary values to real ones.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed the `taint_eviction_controller_pod_deletion_duration_seconds` metric, which recorded nanoseconds scaled by 1e9 instead of seconds. Latencies below about 9.2 seconds fell into the `+Inf` bucket, and longer ones overflowed and were recorded as arbitrary, often negative, values.
```

142192.title: HPA: compute resource utilization ratio without int64 overflow
142192.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig autoscaling

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`GetResourceUtilizationRatio` sums per-pod metric values and requests as raw `int64`, multiplies the metrics total by 100 and narrows to `int32`. All three steps wrap silently. Near `math.MaxInt64` the HPA ends up with a `currentUtilization` of 0 and a negative raw average, and scales the wrong way or not at all.

The two totals are now accumulated exactly with `math/big`, the percentage is taken exactly, and only the final `int32` narrowing is clamped to `math.MaxInt32`/`math.MinInt32`, so an oversized utilization keeps its direction instead of wrapping. The raw average of `int64` values always fits an `int64`, so `rawAverageValue` is unchanged in type and meaning. `GetMetricUsageRatio` had the same unchecked sum and now accumulates the same way. Nothing changes for inputs that fit today and there is no new error path.

Related to #141166 (HPA row of the Quantity int64 overflow burndown; does not close the tracker)

Continues #141978, which GitHub closed on a force-push and refuses to reopen; the two review comments from @jpbetz there (doc comment, and the exact sum in `GetMetricUsageRatio`) are addressed in this head. /cc @jpbetz

The `int32` narrowing saturates rather than returning an error, matching the direction-preserving cap taken for replica counts in #141397. If you would rather the HPA surface an error condition when the percentage does not fit, that is a two-line change and I am happy to make it.

141616.title: cloud-provider: reconcile additional node labels
141616.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`InstanceMetadata.AdditionalLabels` are currently applied only during the initial synchronization of a node carrying the external cloud-provider taint.

Consequently:

* labels introduced by a newer cloud provider are not added to already initialized nodes;
* labels removed from a node are not restored;
* changed values are not updated, leaving provider-specific topology labels stale after operations such as an instance live migration.

This PR introduces the versioned `CloudNodeAdditionalLabelsReconciliation` feature gate, available as Alpha from 1.38 and disabled by default. 142457.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind cleanup

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Moves the gRPC probe from the deprecated `grpc.DialContext` with `WithBlock` to `grpc.NewClient`. The client does no I/O until the health check runs, so the one probe timeout still covers connect and RPC. The target uses the `passthrough` resolver, which hands the address to the probe dialer unresolved, as `DialContext` did by default; `NewClient` would otherwise pick the `dns` resolver. Connection errors now surface from the RPC as `Unavailable` and map to the existing "failed to connect" message.

Behavior change: a refused connection fails the probe at once instead of retrying until `timeoutSeconds`, and a server that never answers reports `timeout: health rpc did not complete within <timeout>` instead of `timeout: failed to connect service`. Probe outcomes do not change.

The unreachable-host test, which asserted the old exact timeout text against port 32, is replaced by a connection-refused test on a closed local port that also checks the probe returns well before its 10s timeout. Precedent: #137955 did the same move for cri-client. The second commit fixes a pre-existing flake in two container lifecycle tests (`exit -1` in busybox) that failed this PR's node e2e run; the comment below has the history.

136991.title: DeepDerivative silently ignores trailing slice item removals
136991.body:
## What happened?

`equality.Semantic.DeepDerivative()` in `k8s.io/apimachinery` does not detect when items are removed from the end of a slice. It only compares up to `len(a)` items (the "desired" side), so any extra trailing items in `b` (the "existing" side) are silently ignored.

This means if a controller uses `DeepDerivative` to determine whether an object needs updating, removing items from the end of a slice (e.g., container args, env vars, volume mounts) will never trigger an update.

## What did you expect to happen?

`DeepDerivative(a, b)` should return `false` when `a` has fewer slice items than `b`, since the desired state differs from the existing state.

## How to reproduce

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/equality"
)

func main() {
	desired := []string{"--foo", "--bar"}
	existing := []string{"--foo", "--bar", "--baz"}

	// Returns true — the removal of "--baz" is NOT detected
	fmt.Println(equality.Semantic.DeepDerivative(desired, existing)) // true
}
```

## Root cause

In `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/conversion/equalities.go`, the `deepDerivative` method has this logic for slices:

```go
for i := range a { // iterates only up to len(a)
    if !e.deepDerivative(a[i], b[i]) {
        return false
    }
}
return true
```

It iterates only over the indices of \`a\` (desired). If \`a\` has 2 items and \`b\` has 3, the third item in \`b\` is never examined.

## Impact

This affects any controller that relies on \`DeepDerivative\` to detect spec changes for reconciliation. Specific real-world impact:

- **[OCPBUGS-65879](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPBUGS-65879)**: In OpenShift HyperShift, removing \`--image-overrides\` arguments from a container's args list was not detected, leaving stale configuration on cluster objects indefinitely.

## Additional context

The trailing slice behavior is **not** documented and appears to be unintentional. 

/sig api-machinery
/kind bug
/area apiserver

140844.title: kubelet copies IPv6 link-local scoped nameservers from the node resolv.conf into pods where they cannot work
140844.body:
### What happened?

With `dnsPolicy: Default`, kubelet copies the node resolv.conf nameservers into the pod verbatim. When the node file contains an IPv6 link-local nameserver with a scope zone, for example `nameserver fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0%3`, that exact line is written into the pod `/etc/resolv.conf`.

The scope zone is a node interface index. It does not exist in the pod network namespace, so the resolver cannot use the address (socket setup fails with `EINVAL`). This also affects CoreDNS, which runs with `dnsPolicy: Default`, inherits the same file, and forwards to it via `forward . /etc/resolv.conf`. Because the forward plugin distributes across all listed nameservers with the default random policy, a fraction of upstream lookups select the unusable server and fail intermittently with resolution timeouts.

Root cause is in `parseResolvConf` (`pkg/kubelet/network/dns/dns.go`). The nameserver value is appended verbatim with no IP parse, address family, scope, or reachability check. The only later processing is truncation to `MaxDNSNameservers` and dedup:

```go
if fields[0] == "nameserver" {
    if len(fields) >= 2 {
        nameservers = append(nameservers, fields[1])
    }
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

kubelet should not propagate a nameserver that cannot function in the pod network namespace. When the pod does not share the host netns, kubelet should drop IPv6 link-local (`fe80::/10`) nameservers that carry a scope zone. This matches the fix Podman shipped in containers/common#2233 for the same case.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Node running systemd-resolved, with kubelet `--resolv-conf=/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf` (the kubeadm default when systemd-resolved is detected).
2. Router advertises IPv6 RDNSS via RA, so systemd-resolved writes a scoped link-local nameserver into that file:
   ```
   nameserver 172.16.3.254
   nameserver fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0%3
   nameserver 2600:1700:76f0:14bf:29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0
   ```
3. Start any pod with `dnsPolicy: Default`. Its `/etc/resolv.conf` contains the `fe80::...%3` line unchanged.
4. From that pod, query the scoped server directly and observe it is unusable in the pod netns:
   ```
   dig @fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0 example.com
   # UDP setup with fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0#53 failed: invalid file
   ```
5. Under normal load, external name resolution fails intermittently as the resolver rotates onto the unusable server.

### Anything else we need to know?

- Precedent that this is a resolv.conf hygiene bug, not expected behavior: containers/common#2233 filters link-local nameservers when building a container resolv.conf, with the reasoning that a container has a different interface index so a scoped address can never work. glibc has long declined to support scoped nameservers (Debian bug 455671).
- Related but distinct: #58180 (pods cannot reach IPv6-only upstreams) and the maintainer note in #54773 that inheriting the host DNS config for pods was likely a mistake.
- The same argument applies to any nameserver kubelet cannot verify is usable from the pod netns, but the concrete and low-risk case is the scoped link-local address.

141212.title: DRA: per-device nodeSelector with multiple terms passes validation and aborts the scheduling cycle
141212.body:
### What happened?

A per-device `nodeSelector` on a ResourceSlice device may contain more than one node selector term.

ResourceSlice API validation accepts such an object, even though the API contract requires exactly one term. When structured allocation selects that device, the allocator rejects the selector with a hard error.

The error is not wrapped with `ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`. The DynamicResources Filter plugin therefore returns a framework Error instead of rejecting only the current node. A Filter error cancels the remaining node search and aborts the current scheduling cycle.

Subsequent retries can reproduce the same failure while the malformed ResourceSlice remains unchanged and allocation continues to select that device.

### Where validation and the allocator disagree

Both node selector fields are documented as single-term selectors:

- `ResourceSliceSpec.NodeSelector`: "Must use exactly one term."
- `Device.NodeSelector`: "Must use exactly one term."

The slice-level selector enforces this contract in `pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go`:

```go
allErrs = append(allErrs,
    corevalidation.ValidateNodeSelector(spec.NodeSelector, false, fldPath.Child("nodeSelector"))...,
)
if len(spec.NodeSelector.NodeSelectorTerms) != 1 {
    allErrs = append(allErrs, field.Invalid(
        fldPath.Child("nodeSelector", "nodeSelectorTerms"),
        spec.NodeSelector.NodeSelectorTerms,
        "must have exactly one node selector term",
    ))
}
```

The per-device path in `validateDevice` only calls `ValidateNodeSelector`:

```go
if device.NodeSelector != nil {
    setFields = append(setFields, "`nodeSelector`")
    allErrs = append(allErrs,
        corevalidation.ValidateNodeSelector(device.NodeSelector, false, fldPath.Child("nodeSelector"))...,
    )
}
```

`ValidateNodeSelector` requires at least one valid term but does not limit the selector to one term. A selector with two or more valid terms therefore passes this validation path.

The allocator later assumes validation has enforced the single-term invariant. In `createNodeSelector`:

```go
default:
    // This shouldn't occur, validation must prevent creation of such slices.
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unsupported ResourceSlice.NodeSelector with %d terms", len(nodeSelector.NodeSelectorTerms))
```

The caller wraps that error with `%w`, but not with `ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`, so the DynamicResources Filter plugin treats it as a fatal framework Error and the scheduler cancels the remaining Filter work for that scheduling cycle. The same `createNodeSelector` branch exists in the stable, incubating, and experimental allocator variants.

### What did you expect to happen?

ResourceSlice API validation should reject a per-device `nodeSelector` whose `nodeSelectorTerms` length is not exactly one, matching the existing validation for `ResourceSliceSpec.NodeSelector`. Malformed ResourceSlices should not be admitted and then deferred until scheduler allocation, where they can abort a scheduling cycle.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Publish a ResourceSlice with `perDeviceNodeSelection: true` and a device whose `nodeSelector` has two individually valid terms (one of them matching a real node), then a ResourceClaim and Pod that select it:

```yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: DeviceClass
metadata:
  name: nsrepro-class
spec:
  selectors:
  - cel:
      expression: 'device.driver == "nsrepro.example"'
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata:
  name: nsrepro-slice
spec:
  driver: nsrepro.example
  pool: {name: nsrepro-pool, generation: 1, resourceSliceCount: 1}
  perDeviceNodeSelection: true
  devices:
  - name: dev0
    attributes:
      type: {string: repro}
    nodeSelector:
      nodeSelectorTerms:                 # two terms; one matches a node in the cluster
      - matchExpressions:
        - {key: kubernetes.io/hostname, operator: In, values: [<a-node-in-your-cluster>]}
      - matchExpressions:
        - {key: kubernetes.io/hostname, operator: In, values: [nonexistent-node]}
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata: {name: nsrepro-claim}
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
    - name: req0
      exactly: {deviceClassName: nsrepro-class, allocationMode: ExactCount, count: 1}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: nsrepro-pod}
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  resourceClaims: [{name: c, resourceClaimName: nsrepro-claim}]
  containers: [{name: c, image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10, resources: {claims: [{name: c}]}}]
```

The ResourceSlice is accepted, confirming API validation does not reject the two-term per-device selector:

```text
deviceclass.resource.k8s.io/nsrepro-class created
resourceslice.resource.k8s.io/nsrepro-slice created
```

The Pod then stays `Pending`, and the scheduler reports it via the Pod event and the kube-scheduler log:

```text
# kubectl get event (Pod nsrepro-pod)
running "DynamicResources" filter plugin: create NodeSelector for claim nsrepro-claim: unsupported ResourceSlice.NodeSelector with 2 terms

# kube-scheduler log
E ... schedule_one.go:279] "Error selecting node for pod" err="running \"DynamicResources\" filter plugin: create NodeSelector for claim nsrepro-claim: unsupported ResourceSlice.NodeSelector with 2 terms" pod="default/nsrepro-pod"
E ... schedule_one.go:1243] "Error scheduling pod; retrying" err="..." logger="UnhandledError" pod="default/nsrepro-pod"
```

The `schedule_one.go:279` "Error selecting node for pod" path (rather than a node-local `Unschedulable` status), and the `UnhandledError` logger, confirm the failure aborts the scheduling cycle rather than filtering out one node.

### Anything else we need to know?

The primary fix appears to be enforcing the same exact-one-term constraint in the per-device validation path in `validateDevice`, plus a regression test in `pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation_resourceslice_test.go`.

For already-stored malformed ResourceSlices, update validation may need to ratchet an unchanged old `nodeSelector` value so that unrelated updates are not blocked. That update-compatibility detail can be handled in the fixing PR.

A defensive allocator change could also be considered for malformed objects that predate the validation fix, but it should not replace enforcement of the API invariant.

### Kubernetes version

Source references (`file:line`) are from master (commit `7f71d2e`). The runtime reproducer above was captured on a real cluster running v1.36.2, where `DRAPartitionableDevices` is Beta and enabled by default (since v1.36).

/kind bug
/sig scheduling
/wg device-management

141274.title: [DRA] ResourceClaim controller can re-reserve terminal Pods
141274.body:
### What happened?

The ResourceClaim controller can oscillate `status.reservedFor` when a terminal, already scheduled Pod still references an allocated static claim that remains in use by another Pod.

The controller has two conflicting paths:

1. `enqueuePod` recognizes a `Succeeded` or `Failed` Pod and queues each referenced claim so terminal reservations can be removed.
2. The same Pod can still satisfy `podNeedsWork` when `spec.nodeName` is set and its allocated claim no longer reserves it.
3. `syncPod` then enters the pre-scheduled-Pod path and restores the terminal Pod's consumer reference.

The claim cleanup path removes that reference again. Under sustained reconciliation this produces repeated `ResourceClaim/status` writes and conflicts while the static allocation remains valid for another consumer.

A manually managed static ResourceClaim shared by multiple Pods is a documented DRA use case; the terminal consumer should be cleanup-only rather than re-reserved.

### What did you expect to happen?

A terminal Pod must never be added or restored to `ResourceClaim.status.reservedFor`.

Claim work should still be enqueued so an existing terminal-Pod reservation is removed. The Pod itself should not be queued for reservation work, and `syncPod` should be safe if an already queued terminal Pod reaches it.

### How can we reproduce it?

A controller unit test can reproduce this with:

1. An allocated, manually managed ResourceClaim.
2. One nonterminal Pod already present in `status.reservedFor`, keeping the allocation live.
3. A second Pod which:
   - references the same claim;
   - has `spec.nodeName` set;
   - is `Succeeded` or `Failed`; and
   - is absent from `status.reservedFor` because cleanup already ran.
4. Sync the terminal Pod key.

On current behavior, the terminal Pod is appended to `reservedFor`. The expected claim status contains only the live consumer.

The minimal correction is to exclude terminal Pods from `podNeedsWork` and to make `syncPod` return before any reservation work. `enqueuePod` already queues referenced claims for terminal-Pod cleanup before applying the Pod work predicate.

### Anything else we need to know?

This was observed as a control-plane hot loop rather than a one-time stale status. A focused regression test fails against Kubernetes `v1.36.2` by showing the extra terminal consumer and passes with the terminal-Pod guard. The complete `pkg/controller/resourceclaim` unit-test package also passes with that correction.

The status field is maintained by Kubernetes core; no DRA vendor-driver behavior is required to reproduce the controller interaction.

/kind bug

142617.title: taint_eviction_controller_pod_deletion_duration_seconds records nanoseconds scaled by 1e9, not seconds
142617.body:
### What happened?

`deletePodHandler` in `pkg/controller/tainteviction/taint_eviction.go` records the pod deletion latency as `float64(time.Since(fireAt) * time.Second)`. `time.Since` already returns nanoseconds, so the multiplication scales the value by another 1e9.

`taint_eviction_controller_pod_deletion_duration_seconds` is documented as "Latency, in seconds" with buckets from 0.005 to 240. Any latency below about 9.2s is recorded as a huge positive number and lands in the `+Inf` bucket. Above about 9.2s the multiplication overflows int64 and wraps around, so the recorded value is arbitrary. For example 10s is recorded as -8446744073709551616 and counts in the lowest bucket, while 20s is recorded as 1553255926290448384. `_sum` is meaningless in all cases.

### What did you expect to happen?

The metric records the latency in seconds, the same way `DeviceTaintEvictionController` does in `pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction.go` with `podDeletionLatency.Seconds()`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Call `deletePodHandler` with a `fireAt` 10s in the past and read the histogram. The regression test in #141742 does this. Before the fix it records -8.44e+18, after the fix about 10.

141631.title: Reconcile cloud-provider InstanceMetadata.AdditionalLabels periodically
141631.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The cloud node controller should periodically reconcile node labels returned through `cloudprovider.InstanceMetadata.AdditionalLabels` for already initialized Nodes.

The reconciliation should:

* add labels that are missing from the Node;
* update labels whose values differ from the current instance metadata;
* preserve unrelated Node labels;
* continue rejecting labels in Kubernetes-reserved namespaces;
* not remove labels that are no longer returned by the cloud provider.

A proposed implementation is available in:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141616

Provider-side implementation:

https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-openstack/pull/3166

Previous implementation attempts:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130888
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131096

### Why is this needed?

`InstanceMetadata.AdditionalLabels` are currently applied only during the initial synchronization of a Node carrying the external cloud-provider taint.

Consequently, labels introduced by a newer cloud provider are not added to already initialized Nodes, manually removed labels are not restored, and changed values remain stale.

One example is the OpenStack `hostId`, which identifies the physical compute host within a project. An OpenStack operator may live-migrate an instance while draining a hypervisor for maintenance. In this case, the provider returns a new `hostId`, but the existing Node label is not updated.

For `InstancesV2` implementations, the cloud node controller already periodically calls `InstanceMetadata()`. Reconciling `AdditionalLabels` therefore does not require an additional cloud-provider API request.

Existing Pods are not automatically rescheduled when a topology label changes. Updating the label still makes the current placement observable and ensures newly scheduled Pods use the current topology information.
